meta.reportLabel: Euro cut to -1: Spain's weekend election threat joined French fiscal stress and EUR/USD hit a 17-month low, making EUR/GBP and EUR/CHF the cleanest shorts.
meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: The board has one story this morning and it is the euro. EUR/USD is 1.11804 and down 0.67%, having touched 1.1161 and a 0.8% loss in Asian hours - the weakest since May 2025, a 17-month low and a fourth consecutive weekly decline. What makes it a regime change rather than another bad day for the euro is that the currency lost ground against all seven of its counterparts: EUR/JPY -0.53%, EUR/CHF -0.52%, EUR/CAD -0.42%, EUR/AUD -0.39%, EUR/GBP -0.38% and EUR/NZD -0.19%. For four weeks this has been a French trade; today it is a euro trade, and the reason is Spain. On Friday October 2 the Spanish Congress rejected two emergency housing decrees, and Prime Minister Sanchez spent the weekend deciding whether to call an early election - if he wants the earliest legally available Sunday, November 29, he has to announce it on Monday October 5, which is today. Polymarket had the probability of an early Spanish election before year-end at 50% as of Friday. That is a second sovereign-political leg on a currency that already carries a French one, and it is what generalised the risk premium. The second thing to get right is what is NOT driving this. The wire framing is that higher US yields are lifting the dollar, and today that is wrong: TradingEconomics has the US ten-year at 5.27% and DOWN 1.4 basis points, after an intraday 5.342% last week that was the highest since 2002. DXY is 102.408 and up 0.47%, but the euro is 57.6% of that index, and the non-euro majors barely moved - GBP/USD -0.26%, USD/CHF +0.15%, USD/JPY +0.12%, USD/CAD +0.23%. This is a euro repricing being read as dollar strength. Third, the franc deserves a correction this report is making explicitly: over the past week the CHF, not the USD, was the best major on the board. USD/CHF fell 0.24% on the week while DXY rose 1.20%, and EUR/CHF is 0.92789, down 1.93% on the week and the lowest since July. That lifts CHF from -1 to 0 and removes several franc-short theses.
meta.nextBigEvent: Pedro Sanchez's decision on an early Spanish election, which has to come as soon as today (October 5) if he wants the earliest legal date of November 29 - the leg that turns the euro's France problem into a euro-bloc problem. Then FOMC minutes on October 7 at 18:00Z, the week's only scheduled US red folder.

dailyRead: Start with the euro, because today it is the only thing on the board that genuinely changed. EUR/USD is 1.11804, down 0.67% on the day and down 1.68% on the week, having traded as low as 1.1161 in Asian hours for a 0.8% loss - the weakest level since May 2025, a 17-month low, and the fourth consecutive weekly decline. On its own that is continuation, not news. What makes this report cut EUR from 0 to -1 is the breadth: the euro lost against every single one of its seven counterparts overnight, with EUR/JPY -0.53%, EUR/CHF -0.52%, EUR/CAD -0.42%, EUR/AUD -0.39%, EUR/GBP -0.38% and EUR/NZD -0.19%. Yesterday this report held EUR at 0 deliberately and said so, on the grounds that French sovereign stress was being offset by a genuinely hawkish inflation picture and that moving the score twice on one set of facts would be noise. The leg that broke overnight is the assumption that the fiscal stress was contained to France. On Friday October 2 the Spanish Congress rejected two emergency housing decrees put forward by Prime Minister Sanchez's Socialist government, a legislative defeat significant enough that he spent the weekend weighing an early general election; if he wants the earliest Sunday the law allows, November 29, the announcement has to be made on Monday October 5 - today. Polymarket priced an early Spanish election before the end of 2026 at 50% as of Friday. Bloomberg's account of the 17-month low names Spain explicitly alongside France. So the euro now carries two sovereign-political legs rather than one, and that is a different instrument to trade than it was yesterday. The French leg has not improved either, though it has not worsened: TradingEconomics closes the French ten-year at 4.8660% against a Bund at 3.4545%, so the OAT-Bund spread is about 141 basis points, unchanged on Friday and still the widest since the 2012 euro-area crisis, with France trading wide of Italy at 4.6110% and Greece at 4.5250%. Prime Minister Lecornu's 2027 draft budget, presented October 1, trims the deficit only from 5.4% to 5.0% of GDP and defers the return to the EU's 3% threshold to 2029, against public debt around 119-121% of GDP, and it faces a divided parliament. Note carefully what the euro is NOT getting from Spain yet: the Spanish ten-year closed Friday at 4.0860%, about 63 basis points over the Bund, which is contained. Today's repricing is happening in the currency, not in Spanish credit. For a 4H trader that cuts both ways - it means the euro is the cleanest expression of the risk, and it means there is no bond-market confirmation yet to lean on. The second thing to get right is what is not driving this, because the wire narrative has it backwards. Several accounts frame the euro's low as a function of US yields lifting the dollar. TradingEconomics, which is canonical here, has the US ten-year at 5.27% and DOWN 1.4 basis points today. The 5.342% figure in circulation was an intraday print last week - the highest since 2002 - not today's level. DXY is 102.408 and up 0.47% on the day, 1.20% on the week and 4.16% year to date, but the euro is 57.6% of that index and the non-euro majors hardly moved: GBP/USD -0.26%, USD/CHF +0.15%, USD/JPY +0.12%, USD/CAD +0.23%, AUD/USD -0.29%, NZD/USD -0.43%. The honest description is a euro repricing being read as dollar strength, which is why USD holds at +2 rather than being marked up. The dollar's own case is unchanged and still rests on December: CME pricing has roughly 80% odds that the Fed holds on October 28 and about 69% odds of a hike by December 9, slightly firmer than the 65% carried yesterday, against September payrolls of 29K versus an 89K forecast, unemployment at 4.2% and average hourly earnings at 0.1% m/m with the y/y down to 3.0%. The September SEP is what keeps the hawkish floor under it - sixteen of eighteen participants want at least one more hike this year, the 2026 median was revised up to 4.1% from 3.8%, and 17 of 18 see PCE inflation risks weighted to the upside. FOMC minutes on October 7 at 18:00Z are the week's only scheduled US red folder and the test of whether December holds. Third, this report is making an explicit correction on the franc, because the tape has been contradicting the score. Over the past week the Swiss franc, not the dollar, was the best-performing major on this board. USD/CHF fell 0.24% on the week at a time when DXY rose 1.20% - the franc gained against a dollar that beat everything else. EUR/CHF is 0.92789, down 1.93% on the week and down 0.52% today, the lowest since July. AUD/CHF fell 1.41% on the week, NZD/CHF 1.62% and CAD/CHF 1.04%. A currency that outperforms the dollar during a dollar-positive week while every risk cross falls against it is not a -1, so CHF moves up to 0 MIXED. What caps it rather than sinks it is unchanged: a 0.00% SNB policy rate against a 5.27% US ten-year, a Swiss ten-year at 0.5250%, and the SNB's restored standard language that it remains willing to intervene in FX as necessary. That upgrade is the reason several crosses change today - USD/CHF comes off LONG to RANGE, GBP/CHF off LONG to RANGE, CHF/JPY off SHORT to RANGE, while EUR/CHF, NZD/CHF, CAD/CHF and AUD/CHF become or stay franc-positive shorts. Sterling is the other side of the cleanest trade on the board and its case firmed again. Bank Rate is 3.75%, held September 17 on a 6-3 vote with three members already preferring 4.00%. The November 5 pricing now runs from about 76% on Polymarket through 83% on overnight index swaps to 87% on the BoE Watch measure, and the genuinely new element is that the economists have caught up with the market: Barclays, UBS and J.P. Morgan all now forecast a November hike. Deputy Governors Breeden and Lombardelli have each set out conditions under which they would vote to raise, and with five of the six September holders having done so, only two need to switch. The pass-through argument stays mechanical rather than market-dependent: UK gas is 190.90 GBp/thm, up 1.49% today, 6.32% on the week and 158.64% year to date, and the domestic unit rate stepped up about 27% year on year on October 1. The gilt ten-year is 5.37%, above the US ten-year, near a two-decade high. The soft leg is labour - employment change +67K and falling, the payroll proxy at -26.1K - which is why GBP holds at +2 rather than going higher. Four MPC speakers this week, Mann, Greene and Pill on October 6 and Lombardelli on October 8, with October 20 earnings and October 21 CPI the real gates before November 5. The yen is cut from +1 to 0 and the reason is specific rather than atmospheric. The Bank of Japan's September Summary of Opinions, published last week, fell short of the hawkish signalling the market wanted, and USD/JPY pushed past 158 to one-month yen lows; it is 158.041 this morning. The twelve-month path has not changed - money markets still price roughly 90 basis points of cumulative hikes, the policy rate is 1.25% after the 7-2 September 18 hike with Asada and Sato dissenting, and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7% against a 2.4% forecast with the core-core gauge at 3.0% - so this is not a dovish reassessment, it is the removal of a near-term premium that the Summary of Opinions did not justify. October 29-30 dispersion remains wide and December remains the better base case. Governor Ueda speaks tomorrow, October 6 at 06:35Z, and it is the week's first red folder and the single scheduled chance to put October back on the table. The structural drag is unmoved: 1.25% against a 5.27% US ten-year is still the worst funding disadvantage here, and a JGB ten-year at 3.0930% has not closed it. For context on how much work the authorities have done, the Ministry of Finance deployed a record 11.73 trillion yen across April and May, and coordinated intervention lifted the yen from beyond 163 to around 157. Commodities carry the day's second real change. WTI broke below ninety dollars, at 89.994 and down 1.22% on the day and 2.81% on the week, while Brent held 101.472, down 0.76% on the day but still up 3.72% on the week. That widens the WTI-Brent spread to about 11.48 dollars, and the widening is the tradeable part rather than the level. The G7, IEA and partner release of up to 100 million barrels agreed October 2 is front-loaded over the first twenty days with a heavy diesel component, and it lands on the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve and refined products - the WTI complex - rather than on waterborne crude, which still carries the Hormuz premium. The Strait remains effectively closed, with transits running at roughly a third below the prior week, vessels using Iran-designated routes under threat of armed response, and IEA cumulative supply losses now past a billion barrels. So USOIL moves from RANGE to SHORT as a location and structure call, not a bearish-oil call, and the risk on it is obvious: any Hormuz escalation closes that spread violently. It is consistent with CAD at -1, where the terms-of-trade benefit accrues to Brent while Canada sells into the discounted barrel. Canada's own week is the only one on this board carrying red-folder figures - September employment on October 9 at 12:30Z, consensus +9.0K after -41.7K, with the unemployment rate seen rising to 6.5% from 6.4%. The overnight rate is 2.25%, a 175 basis point gap to the Fed's upper bound. Gold and silver have stopped falling, which is enough to retire two shorts. Gold is 4136.39, down 0.09% today but UP 0.52% on the week against a month that is still down 6.10% and a year down 4.25%; silver is 60.995, up 1.04% today and 0.61% on the week against a month down 7.78%, and it is outperforming gold as its industrial leg reasserts. A ten-year that eased to 5.27% from a 5.342% peak is what did it. Neither metal has turned - the monthly damage is real and the Fed is still the hostile axis - but a short whose weekly momentum has flipped positive is a RANGE, not a SHORT, and saying so is more useful than defending yesterday's call. Copper is 6.5156, up 0.36% today but down 0.82% on the week and 3.32% on the month, and it still refuses to confirm the Australian story even with BHP's Escondida halted since September 23 and supervisors having voted 95% to authorise a strike; AUD stays at 0 with a 4.60% cash rate, August CPI at 4.0% and a November 3 meeting the market has at roughly one in three. New Zealand stays at -1 and the weakest on the board: NZD/USD -0.43% today and -4.89% on the month, an OCR of 2.75% a full point below the Fed's upper bound even if October 28 delivers, and a Q3 CPI on October 21 that is a clean test against the Bank's own published 3.9% forecast. Equities are the one place the euro's trouble is not showing: DE40 is 25,214.00 and up 1.17%, EU50 6,237.30 and up 1.02%, with the Spanish ES35 up 22.46% year to date and Italy's IT40 up 16.70%. That is why EU50 comes off a SHORT it was not earning - periphery equity is rallying through the same sovereign stress that is sinking the currency, and the bank weight is the reason. GER40 goes the other way to a modest LONG, where the weak-euro translation leg and sub-ninety WTI are currently beating the gas leg, with German gas at 75.77 EUR/MWh and up 3.98% on the week. The clean trades: EUR/GBP short at 0.84663 remains the highest-conviction idea on the board with both legs now moving the right way, EUR/CHF short at 0.92789 is the new one and the franc upgrade is what unlocks it, GBP/NZD long at 2.36199 is the widest policy spread available, and EUR/USD short is the momentum expression with the caveat that part of today's move was mechanical. Not financial advice.

USD.when: December 9, with October 28 effectively priced out - CME has roughly 80% odds of a hold this month and about 69% odds the target range is higher after December, slightly firmer than the 65% carried yesterday
USD.note: TE re-verified: the upper bound of the fed funds target range is 4.00%, raised from 3.75% on September 16 in a unanimous decision, the first increase since 2023. Today's job is to separate the dollar's own case from the euro's collapse, because they are being conflated. The US ten-year is 5.27% on TE and DOWN 1.4 basis points; the 5.342% figure in circulation was an intraday print last week and the highest since 2002, not a current level. DXY at 102.408 and up 0.47% is mostly the 57.6% euro weight doing the work. The hawkish floor is the September SEP, read from the Board's own projections table: four participants at a 4.375% 2026 midpoint, twelve at 4.125% and two at 3.875%, so sixteen of eighteen want at least one more hike this year and four want two. The 2026 median was revised up to 4.1% from 3.8% in June, 2027 is 4.1%, 2028 is 3.9% and the longer run 3.2%. PCE is projected at 3.7% for 2026 with core at 3.4%, GDP at 2.3% and unemployment at 4.1%. The risk assessment is the most hawkish element: 17 of 18 see PCE inflation risks to the upside and 15 of 18 the same for core. Chair Warsh again declined to submit forecasts. Against that, September payrolls printed 29K against an 89K forecast with August revised to 133K, unemployment 4.2% against 4.1% expected, average hourly earnings 0.1% m/m with the y/y easing to 3.0%, and core PCE on September 30 soft at 0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y against 3.3% expected. FOMC minutes on October 7 at 18:00Z are the week's only scheduled US red folder and the question is whether they confirm the dovish read of the payroll miss or restate the tightening bias; ISM services lands today at 14:00Z with a 55.1 forecast, claims October 8 and UoM sentiment October 9. September CPI on October 14 at 12:30Z is the real gate for December.

EUR.when: December is the base case and October 29 is live but not favoured; the constraint is now political rather than monetary, with Spain's election risk added to France's budget arithmetic
EUR.note: TE re-verified: the ECB deposit facility rate is 2.50%, raised from 2.25% on September 10 - TE's main refinancing rate row reads 2.65%, which is not the rate this board tracks. September flash HICP was 3.8% y/y, the highest since September 2023, up from a downward-revised 3.2% and above a 3.6-3.7% consensus, with core at 2.5% from 2.4%; energy's annual rate surged to 18.8% from 14.3%, worth about 1.7 percentage points of the headline at roughly 9% of the basket. On inflation alone a pause is hard to justify, which is why the path stays at hike. What changed over the weekend is the politics, and it broadened. Spain's Congress rejected two emergency housing decrees on Friday October 2, and Prime Minister Sanchez has to announce an early election on Monday October 5 if he wants the earliest legal Sunday of November 29; Polymarket had an early Spanish election before year-end at 50% as of Friday. France is unchanged but unresolved: TE closes the French ten-year at 4.8660% against a Bund at 3.4545%, about 141 basis points and still the widest since the 2012 crisis, with France wide of Italy at 4.6110% and Greece at 4.5247%. Lecornu's 2027 draft budget of October 1 trims the deficit only from 5.4% to 5.0% of GDP, defers the 3% threshold to 2029 and faces a divided parliament, against debt around 119-121% of GDP. The important distinction for trading it: Spain's ten-year closed at 4.0860%, only about 63 basis points over the Bund, so this is so far a currency repricing rather than a credit one, and there is no bond confirmation yet to lean on. TE's ECB summary records Lagarde putting growth risks to the downside and inflation risks to the upside with decisions meeting by meeting, the 2026 inflation forecast held at 3.0%, 2027 revised to 2.5% and 2028 to 2.1%, and growth upgraded to 0.9% for 2026. The accounts of the September 10 meeting publish October 8 at 11:30Z and are the best scheduled read on how close the Council is to pausing; Nagel speaks today. The decision is October 29 at 13:15Z with the press conference at 13:45Z.

GBP.when: November 5, and the new element is that the forecasters have caught up with the market: Barclays, UBS and J.P. Morgan all now call a hike, against pricing of 76% on Polymarket, 83% on swaps and 87% on the BoE Watch measure
GBP.note: TE re-verified: Bank Rate is 3.75%, held at the September 17 decision on a 6-3 vote with three members preferring 4.00%, the same split as July. TE's summary records the MPC saying prolonged Middle East conflict has pushed energy prices higher and contributed to UK CPI rising to 3.1% in August, with further increases expected in coming quarters, and that policy must ensure inflation returns sustainably to 2% while the Committee assesses the scale and duration of the energy shock; it notes limited evidence so far of significant second-round effects, with that risk increasing if energy costs stay elevated. The MPC also unanimously agreed to run the gilt stock to zero over a multi-year programme at an average GBP46 billion a year through 2034. The vote arithmetic is what makes November live: Deputy Governor Breeden has said a hike would be appropriate if second-round effects crystallise and Deputy Governor Lombardelli that the case is building, and both voted to hold in September, so with five of the six holders having set out conditions only two need to switch. LSEG data has four hikes priced by July 2027. The energy pass-through is mechanical rather than market-dependent: UK gas is 190.90 GBp/thm, up 1.49% today, 6.32% on the week and 158.64% year to date, and the domestic unit rate stepped from 6.29p to 8p per kWh on October 1, about 27% higher year on year. The gilt ten-year is 5.37%, above the US ten-year at 5.27% and near a two-decade high. The soft leg that caps the score is labour: employment change +67K and falling, and TE's payroll proxy at -26.1K. Four MPC speakers this week - Mann October 6 at 08:30Z, Greene at 09:15Z and Pill at 10:30Z, then Lombardelli at 13:00Z on October 8, one of the two swing votes. October 20 average earnings and October 21 CPI settle it before November 5 at 12:00Z.

JPY.when: October 29-30 is live but not favoured and December is the better base case; last week's Summary of Opinions removed the near-term premium rather than the path, and twelve-month pricing still carries roughly 90 basis points
JPY.note: TE re-verified: the policy rate is 1.25% after the September 18 hike, the highest since April 1995, taken 7-2 with Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissenting - just three months after the previous increase, the shortest interval between BoJ hikes since 1990, and following pressure from Washington including calls from US Treasury Secretary Bessent for higher rates. TE notes most policymakers signalled support for further increases and that the Bank expects inflation above 2% in coming years. What changed last week is the near-term read: the September Summary of Opinions fell short of the hawkish signalling the market wanted and USD/JPY pushed past 158 to one-month yen lows, and it is 158.041 this morning. That is the specific fact behind cutting JPY from +1 to 0 - it removes a premium the document did not justify rather than reversing the direction, because the twelve-month path is intact at roughly 90 basis points of cumulative hikes and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7% against a 2.4% forecast with the core-core gauge at 3.0%. The October 30 meeting carries a fresh quarterly Outlook Report, still the natural vehicle for a hike the Bank wants its own forecasts to justify. Governor Ueda speaks tomorrow, October 6 at 06:35Z - the week's first red folder and the one scheduled chance to put October back on the table - with average cash earnings the same day at 23:30Z. The structural drag is unchanged: 1.25% against a 5.27% US ten-year is the worst funding disadvantage on this board and a JGB ten-year at 3.0930% has not closed it. For scale on official resistance, the Ministry of Finance deployed a record 11.73 trillion yen across April and May and coordinated intervention lifted the yen from beyond 163 to around 157, so the 158 area is where verbal risk starts to matter again.

AUD.when: November 3, where markets have had roughly one in three since the September 29 hike; Q3 CPI on October 28 at 00:30Z resolves it
AUD.note: TE re-verified: the cash rate is 4.60% after a unanimous September 29 hike, the fourth of 2026 and the highest since 2011. TE's summary records the Board noting that higher global energy prices following oil supply disruptions amid the Middle East conflict, stronger-than-expected recent inflation and persistent domestic capacity constraints are adding to inflation, with AI-related demand lifting global technology goods prices and firms reporting rising costs and plans to pass them on; output growth slowed but was slightly stronger than expected in Q2 while consumer spending is easing, housing prices fell in most capital cities and labour market conditions have now also eased. The Board said further tightening may be needed to prevent inflation becoming embedded. The data behind it: monthly CPI 4.0% y/y for August against a 4.1% forecast and 3.5% prior with the trimmed mean at 3.6%, both above the 2-3% band; unemployment 4.6% from 4.5%; August employment +39,493; wage growth 3.2%; annual GDP 2.1% from 2.5%. The commodity leg still will not confirm, and a fifth day of holding AUD at 0 rests on it. Supporting data: unemployment 5.6% from 5.4%, Q2 employment +0.5%, annual GDP 2.6% from 1.7%, core inflation 3.2%, wage growth 2.1%. catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz and the G7 reserve release
catalysts.note: The Strait remains effectively closed, with transits roughly a third below the prior week, vessels using Iran-designated routes, and IEA cumulative supply losses past a billion barrels. Against that, the October 2 G7 and IEA release of up to 100 million barrels is front-loaded over twenty days onto the US reserve and refined products. The tension between the two is the $11.48 WTI-Brent spread.

OAT-Bund is about 141bp with France wide of Italy at 4.6110% and Greece at 4.5247%, while Spain's ten-year is only about 63bp over the Bund. The euro is repricing political risk in the currency ahead of the credit market, which is both the opportunity and the caveat.

geopolitics: The oil transmission changed shape over the weekend rather than changing level, and the shape is what trades. The Strait of Hormuz is still effectively closed: transits are running roughly a third below the prior week, the vessels that do move are using Iran-designated routes under threat of armed response with some running AIS-dark, and IEA cumulative supply losses are now past a billion barrels. That is the structural bid under crude and it has not weakened. What has changed is where the relief is landing. The G7, the IEA and partner countries agreed on October 2 to release up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over four months, front-loaded into the first twenty days with a heavy refined-product component, and those barrels come out of the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve and product stocks rather than out of waterborne crude. The market has now priced that distinction explicitly: WTI broke below ninety dollars overnight to 89.994, down 1.22% on the day and 2.81% on the week, while Brent held 101.472 and is still up 3.72% on the week despite falling 0.76% today. The WTI-Brent spread is therefore about 11.48 dollars and widening, which is the single most tradeable consequence of the release and the reason USOIL moves to SHORT as a location call rather than a bearish-oil call. Gas is the leg that has not been relieved at all, and it is the inflation engine for Europe. EU gas is 76.14 EUR/MWh and up 1.74% today, 6.71% on the week and 170.36% year to date; German gas is 75.77 and up 3.98% on the week; UK gas is 190.90 GBp/thm and up 1.49% today, 6.32% on the week and 158.64% year to date. The FX read follows from the asymmetry. Canada is short the barrel that is falling and long nothing - the discount is in exactly the complex it sells into - which keeps CAD at -1 ahead of September employment on October 9. Sterling is the clearest beneficiary of the gas leg, because the pass-through is mechanical rather than market-dependent after the domestic unit rate stepped up about 27% year on year on October 1, and it is why the MPC's own September statement flagged energy as the reason CPI reached 3.1% with further increases expected; that is the inflation argument behind a November 5 hike now priced at 76-87% and forecast by Barclays, UBS and J.P. Morgan. The euro gets the worst of both: it imports the gas shock into a 3.8% HICP that would normally be hawkish, but it cannot monetise that hawkishness while its sovereign bloc carries a French budget it cannot pass and a Spanish government that may be heading for a November 29 election. That combination - imported inflation plus political paralysis - is what pushed the euro to a 17-month low against all seven counterparts and what sent the intra-European haven bid into the franc, which beat even the dollar last week. For the dollar, the energy premium is a yield story that is currently resting: the ten-year eased to 5.27% today after an intraday 5.342% last week, the highest since 2002, which is also what let gold and silver stop falling. Equities are taking the oil relief rather than the gas threat for now, with DE40 up 1.17% and EU50 up 1.02%, and the periphery indices up far more year to date than the DAX. Not financial advice.
